content: Gluten-related disorders encompass all conditions triggered by gluten consumption. These include celiac disease and non-celiac gluten sensitivity (NCGS). Historically, terms like gluten intolerance and gluten sensitivity have been used interchangeably, either as umbrella terms or specifically for NCGS. Symptoms of gluten-related disorders can include bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, muscle disturbances, headaches, migraines, severe acne, fatigue, and bone or joint pain. Additionally, other components of wheat, apart from gluten, may contribute to symptoms, raising questions about gluten's role in functional bowel disorders like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Gluten, derived from the Latin word for glue, provides elasticity to dough, aiding in its rise and shape retention. It is a common component of many staple foods in Western diets. In 2011, an expert panel in London classified gluten-related disorders into three categories: autoimmune disorders (e.g., celiac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, gluten ataxia), non-autoimmune and non-allergic disorders (e.g., NCGS, likely immune-modulated), and allergic conditions (e.g., wheat allergy, wheat-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis, baker's asthma, contact dermatitis). Autoimmune gluten-related disorders include celiac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, and gluten ataxia. Research indicates that early diagnosis and treatment with a gluten-free diet in gluten ataxia patients can improve symptoms and prevent progression. Patients with gluten ataxia and other neurological conditions often exhibit a different HLA distribution, particularly a higher prevalence of HLA-DQ1, compared to typical celiac disease patients. Non-celiac gluten sensitivity (NCGS) was defined in 2009 by Verdu et al. as a condition involving immunological, morphological, or symptomatic manifestations that may overlap with celiac disease and IBS. NCGS is considered when gluten reactivity is present, but celiac disease and wheat allergy are excluded. While NCGS symptoms resemble those of celiac disease, they are generally less severe and lack anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies or autoimmune comorbidities. However, in 2013, Biesiekierski et al. suggested that NCGS might not be a distinct entity and that its effects could be confounded by FODMAP restriction. They proposed that low-gluten diets might alleviate gastrointestinal symptoms by reducing FODMAPs rather than gluten itself. This has led to debates about the existence of NCGS as a discrete condition. Despite this, NCGS, potentially immune-mediated, appears to be more common than celiac disease. Other conditions associated with gluten include increased α-gliadin antibodies in non-celiac individuals with oral ulcers and in subsets of patients with pseudo-exfoliation syndrome or Sjögren's syndrome. Among Sjögren's syndrome patients with gluten reactivity, only a minority have confirmed celiac disease or gluten-sensitive enteropathy, while others may exhibit gluten sensitivity. All these individuals are HLA-DQ2 and/or DQ8-positive. Over 250 symptoms of gluten sensitivity have been reported, including gastrointestinal issues like bloating, abdominal pain, constipation, and diarrhea, as well as extraintestinal symptoms such as headaches, brain fog, tingling or numbness in extremities, fatigue, muscle disturbances, bone or joint pain, and neuropsychiatric manifestations (e.g., gluten-sensitive idiopathic neuropathies). The etiology of gluten-related disorders varies. In early childhood, enteropathy leads to more rapid symptomatic disease onset. In older populations, celiac disease incidence is higher than in the general population. Allergic diseases may fluctuate with age, and factors like non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug use may increase the risk of urticaria or anaphylaxis. NCGS may have a late onset, with a median age of 55 years and a higher prevalence in females. A double-blind placebo-controlled trial found that gluten exacerbated symptoms like pain, fatigue, bloating, and stool inconsistency in IBS patients, but follow-up studies found no significant differences between gluten and placebo groups. The immunochemistry of gluten involves innate immune responses, HLA-DQ-mediated antigen presentation, killer cell stimulation, and antibody recognition. Responses vary by type of gluten sensitivity and are influenced by genetic factors, particularly HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8. In celiac disease, recognition mechanisms include innate immunity, HLA-DQ presentation, and antibody recognition of gliadin and transglutaminase. In NCGS, elevated AGA IgG is common, while wheat allergy involves IgE-mediated responses to gliadin and other wheat proteins. The pathophysiology of NCGS is less understood than that of celiac disease. A 2014 review described NCGS patients as a heterogeneous group with varying pathogeneses, clinical histories, and courses. Genetically, celiac disease and NCGS are linked to HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genes on chromosome 6p21. Nearly all celiac patients are HLA-DQ2/DQ8-positive, but the specificity of these markers for celiac disease is low. About 50% of NCGS patients carry these alleles, a higher proportion than in the general population. Complications of gluten-related disorders include an increased risk of lymphoid cancers in individuals with anti-gliadin antibodies (AGA), whether diagnosed or untreated. Diagnosis of NCGS requires exclusion of celiac disease and wheat allergy. Celiac disease diagnosis involves serological testing for IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) and anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA), with duodenal biopsy confirmation if serology is positive. HLA-DQ typing can help exclude celiac disease, especially in patients already on a gluten-free diet. A four-of-five rule has been proposed for celiac disease diagnosis, requiring four of the following: typical symptoms, positive serum autoantibodies, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotypes, small bowel biopsy evidence, and response to a gluten-free diet. Treatment for celiac disease involves a lifelong strict gluten-free diet. For NCGS, the duration and strictness of the diet remain uncertain. Wheat allergy patients typically follow a gluten-free diet for six years, except those with anaphylaxis, who require lifelong wheat avoidance. Gluten-free diets should not be initiated before diagnostic testing for celiac disease, as serological and biopsy tests are reliable only when gluten is consumed. Newly diagnosed celiac patients benefit from dietitian support to identify hidden gluten sources, plan balanced meals, and navigate food shopping and dining. Gluten-free diets can lack essential nutrients and be high in fat and calories, so balanced eating is crucial. Gluten-free oats can provide fiber, vitamin B, iron, zinc, and complex carbohydrates, but their introduction should be delayed for a year post-diagnosis due to risks like avenin-sensitive enteropathy (ASE) and contamination issues. The prevalence of celiac disease and wheat allergy is approximately 1% each, while NCGS affects 6% of the population. In Europe, average daily gluten consumption ranges from 10g to 20g, with some individuals consuming over 50g. Regulations for gluten-free food labeling vary by country. In Europe, harmonized rules for labeling gluten-free and very low gluten foods were established in 2009 and later updated. The crossed-grain symbol, a trademarked logo, helps patients with gluten-related disorders identify gluten-free packaged foods.
